new.title: Capability manifest entry authored with an extra 'note' field the strict schema forbids
new.cause: The agent wrote a free-text 'note' field on a capability entry in a PRD capability manifest. CapabilityManifestDoc rejects unknown keys (extra_forbidden), so the manifest failed to load. The schema's allowed fields were not checked before authoring, and the failure only surfaced when a validation script was run ad hoc. A wrong manifest would block the next change that consumes it.

verdict.severity_reason: The error is loud and fixed by deleting one key, but it appears only when a validator is run ad hoc, after authoring.
verdict.reason: In the live reify manifests, `note:` is a task-level key. For example, `docs/prds/alpha-spine.capability-manifest.yaml` has `note:` beside `label`, `task_id` and `title` on lines 5-8. A capability entry carries `name`, `binding`, `verdict` and `delivered_check`, and no `note` (lines 9-17). `.claude/skills/prd/project.md` documents manifest landing and evidence forms, but a search of it found no `capabilities:`, `delivered_checks:` or schema text, so it does not say which keys a capability entry allows. I could not read `CapabilityManifestDoc` in this tree, so the `extra_forbidden` rejection is taken from the evidence. I did not find the failing manifest from the session. The 18 yaml manifests with task-level `note:` make an agent likely to copy it onto a capability.
verdict.proposal: In the capability-manifest authoring section, list the exact allowed keys for a task entry (which includes `note`) and for a capability entry (`name`, `binding`, `verdict`, `delivered_check`), say that unknown keys are rejected as extra_forbidden, and tell the author to put free-text caveats in the task-level `note` or in `binding`.

new.title: npm install in a scratch gui copy fails with an arborist 'edgesOut' null-dereference after node_modules is deleted by hand
new.cause: The agent ran `rm -rf node_modules packages/shared-utils/node_modules` and then `npm install` in a scratch copy of gui. npm crashed with an internal arborist error, `Cannot read properties of null (reading 'edgesOut')`, and no node_modules/.bin/vitest was produced. The reify project's documented self-provisioning path is `scripts/gui-test.sh`, which runs `npm ci --prefer-offline`. The scratch-copy workflow had no known-good install recipe, so the agent kept retrying install variants (the log name 'npm-install-v4b' suggests several attempts) and could not run vitest.

verdict.severity_reason: Contained tooling friction. Agents have a canonical path in gui-test.sh, and the failure only affects an off-path scratch-copy workflow.
verdict.reason: The documented install path exists and works: /home/leo/src/reify/scripts/gui-test.sh runs `npm ci --prefer-offline` in the repo's own gui/. gui/package.json depends on the local workspace package `@reify/shared-utils` at gui/packages/shared-utils, so deleting both node_modules directories by hand and running `npm install` in a copy is a plausible trigger for the arborist `edgesOut` crash. Nothing in the tree gives a recipe for running vitest from a scratch copy of gui. The script header only covers the lane/worktree case, where it uses the repo-root path. The crash itself is npm-internal, and I could not reproduce it here, so I did not confirm the root cause. The observable part is that a recipe is missing.
verdict.proposal: Add a short usage note to the header saying scratch copies of gui should be provisioned with `npm ci --prefer-offline` (never hand-deleted node_modules plus `npm install`) or by running this script from the repo root.

new.title: run_all.sh hangs on one unfinished member until the outer timeout, and the summary names no failing member
new.cause: The infra pool stalled at 195/196 complete for hundreds of seconds, and the 30m outer timeout then killed the run. The resulting summary reads 'FAILED:  (partial)' with an empty failing-name field, and the block reason is only 'tests failed [category: test_failure]'. The stuck member is not identified in the failure text, so the next agent has to dig through a roughly 1.17M-character log to find which member hung. A timeout caused by a hung member is also categorized the same way as a real test failure.

verdict.severity_reason: A hung infra member costs the next agent a search through a very large log, but the cost is contained: the run is still marked failed and only diagnosis is slowed.
verdict.reason: The current tests/infra/run_all.sh still behaves as the cluster describes. The SIGTERM handler `_ra_on_term` builds its failed-name list only from members whose `.rc` file records a nonzero exit, plus `failed_names`. A member that is still running and has no `.rc` file is therefore never named, so a hung member gives `=== FAILED:  (partial) ===` and a bare `FAILED (partial)` line. The header comment calls the empty-names case DELIBERATE and justifies it by over-classifying an interrupt as a failure. The pool progress heartbeat prints only `X/Y complete, elapsed Ns` and does not list which members are pending. Nothing in this file separates a hang from a real test failure, and the cause lies in no other file in this tree. I did not read verify.sh or dark-factory's classifier, so I did not check the 'tests failed [category: test_failure]' block reason or the 1.17M-character log.
verdict.proposal: In `_ra_on_term` and the progress heartbeat, list the pool members that have no `.rc` file (still in flight) and print them, for example as `=== IN-FLIGHT at interrupt: <names> ===`, so a hung member is named in the output.

new.observation: Heuristic 10, clear invariants informatively, redundantly, uniformly enforced: the manifest schema enforces its key set loudly (extra_forbidden names the offending key), but enforcement is single-point and late. Nothing checks at authoring time, so the invariant reaches the author only when a validator is run by hand, after the manifest is written. Heuristic 11, SPOT: the allowed key set for a capability entry lives only in CapabilityManifestDoc, and the authoring guidance in .claude/skills/prd/project.md neither restates it nor points at it, so the author has two sources that disagree by omission. Heuristic 13, files make internal sense in isolation: a reader of the authoring doc cannot tell from that file alone that a task entry allows `note` while a capability entry does not, and the 18 live manifests carrying task-level `note:` make the wrong generalisation the natural one. The fix is in the proposal: name both key sets where the author reads, and say unknown keys are rejected.

Heuristic 11, SPOT: the project has exactly one install recipe, `npm ci --prefer-offline` in scripts/gui-test.sh, but that recipe is reachable only by running the script from the repo root, and its header describes only the lane/worktree case. An agent working in a scratch copy of gui has no stated path and improvises, which is how a hand-deleted node_modules followed by `npm install` reaches npm's arborist crash. Heuristic 13, files make internal sense in isolation: gui/package.json depends on the local workspace package @reify/shared-utils at gui/packages/shared-utils, so a copy of gui is not self-describing as an installable unit; the dependency on a sibling path is what a hand-cleaned `npm install` trips over. The crash itself is npm-internal and was not reproduced; the observable defect is the missing recipe for the off-path case, and the proposed header note closes it.

Heuristic 10, clear invariants informatively enforced: on SIGTERM, `_ra_on_term` builds its failed-name list only from members whose `.rc` file records a nonzero exit, so a member still in flight has no `.rc` and is never named. The run is correctly marked failed, but the message `=== FAILED:  (partial) ===` names no offending value, and the heartbeat prints only `X/Y complete` with no pending list. Heuristic 12, structured data instead of meaningful strings: the outcome reaches the next agent as an empty name slot inside a summary line and a block reason of `tests failed [category: test_failure]`, so a hang and a genuine failure collapse into the same string and the distinction has to be recovered by reading a very large log. The header comment labels the empty-names case deliberate; that choice over-classifies an interrupt rather than reporting what is known at interrupt time, which the proposal corrects by printing the in-flight members by name.

findings.statement: The agent ran `git log` and `ls` on `scripts/main-gate-mark.sh`, a filename it inferred from the identifier `main_gate_mark` in a commit subject. The file does not exist, so `ls` exited 2. The commit subject names a function, not a file path. The implementation lives elsewhere, and the sentinel is marked by the hook-gated commit path. A bare `ls` of a guessed path gives no pointer to the real location, so the agent has to search again. Verifier: scripts/main-gate-mark.sh exists in the current tree. It is an executable file, and `git log` shows commits touching it, including 883d277c68 'main_gate_mark removes its temp file when the publish fails'. The `ls` failure in the claim (exit 2, no such file) does not reproduce here. The agent most likely ran it in a worktree or lane checkout that lacked the file. That cause is not something I can observe from this tree.

The agent passed `--short` with both HEAD and main to a single `git rev-parse`. With `--short` the command takes exactly one revision, so it died with 'Needed a single revision'. Because the call was the head of an && chain, the later `wc -l` and `tail` steps never ran. Revealing the end of the deliberation plan file therefore needed another round trip. Verifier: The cluster describes a one-off agent mistake: `git rev-parse --short HEAD main` takes exactly one revision with `--short`, so the call exits 128 and the rest of the && chain is skipped. This is git's own behavior and a transient shell-command error. It is not a fact about the current state of /home/leo/src/reify. I did not read any file in the tree to check this. Nothing in the tree produces, teaches, or fails to guard against it.

The agent built a get_task_escalations call with an empty value for the optional 'status' field, so the JSON was invalid. It sent the same malformed payload again at turn 63 instead of omitting the field or supplying a value, so the error text did not change its behavior. Verifier: The malformed call (`"status": ,`) came from the agent while it was building an `mcp__escalation__get_task_escalations` call. That tool is defined and served by dark-factory, not by this tree. A grep for `get_task_escalations` finds it only in confusion-codebook and census artifacts (docs/legibility/confusion-codebook.yaml and two plans/confusion-census-2026-10-30 files). No source, schema or prompt in /home/leo/src/reify defines the tool or teaches this call shape, so there is no current fact here to verify and no existing file to fix.

Agent waits for a long-running cargo test suite and GUI run by re-issuing near-identical grep/tail poll commands on the log file (47 times for one log, 5 for another), with the session ending before the final poll returned. There is no completion-marker wait primitive in use, so each poll burns a turn and context, and the session ended with step-4 still pending. Verifier: The cluster describes one agent session's behaviour: 47 near-identical grep/tail polls on /tmp/t6690-step4-full3.log. The session transcript is not part of the reify tree, so I can't confirm it as a fact about the current tree. The cause is how the agent runs its Bash tool (foreground polling instead of a background run or Monitor wait), and that tooling is not in this tree. The tree already points agents at purpose-built waits (scripts/await-merge-landing.py for merges, scripts/cargo-test-tally.py for counting a run once from a captured file). No existing file in the tree produces or teaches this polling pattern, and I found no specific file to name for a remediation. The one check I ran was a grep of cargo-test-tally.py for polling or background-wait guidance, which found nothing.

The agent guessed the add_plan_step signature. It passed task_id, which the tool does not accept, and omitted the required step_id. Validation rejected the call before anything ran, so a retry was safe, but the agent had no schema in view and wasted a turn. Verifier: The only mentions of add_plan_step in /home/leo/src/reify are the census records: docs/legibility/confusion-codebook.yaml and the plans/confusion-census-*.md and .json files. Nothing in the tree defines the tool's schema or teaches agents to call it. The tool belongs to the dark-factory plan-tools MCP server, which this tree does not contain. The codebook already lists about ten near-identical candidates under the anchor slug:plan-tools-add-plan-step-schema-guessing, and most are marked rejected. The one fact the tree does show is that agents have called the tool with guessed argument names. I can't tie that to any file here that produces or fails to guard against it.

A held leaf contract (S9 lambda) says RelationInstance is 'parsed once by the compiler'. In the code it lives in reify-constraints and is built in reify-eval's relate_solve.rs::relation_instance. The PRD wording was never checked against the code's actual ownership before decomposition. An agent implementing the leaf from that contract would look in the compiler and put the work in the wrong crate or stage. The mismatch only surfaced when a recon seat read the code. Verifier: The code facts are right: `RelationInstance` is defined in crates/reify-constraints/src/relate_solve.rs and has one construction site, `relation_instance` in crates/reify-eval/src/relate_solve.rs. But the PRD no longer holds the claimed wrong wording. The only 'parsed once by the compiler' left in docs/ is docs/prds/v0_6/compiler-declaration-passes.md line 200, struck through and marked 'superseded by R6'. The amendment on that row binds `reify_builtins::RelationKind` instead. The kinematics PRD (line 159) and its capability manifest name the same ownership: the type is in reify-constraints, and the only construction site is `reify_eval::relate_solve::relation_instance`. The remaining 'parsed once by the compiler' occurrences are in review proposal JSON and plan files, not in contracts. I did not find the S9 λ contract text. The stale wording was corrected in the docs, so it is no longer an observable fact about the current tree.

The agent wrote `tail -3` in a compound final-verification command (likely with multiple files or after other arguments). GNU tail only accepts the obsolete `-N` form when it is the sole or first option, so it failed with 'option used in invalid context'. The whole command exited 1 even though the ratchet and guard checks both reported rc=0. This makes a successful verification look like a failure and forces a re-run. Verifier: The cluster describes a one-off ad-hoc shell mistake: an agent ran `tail -3` in an invalid position in a command it composed itself. The GNU tail error appears only in a session log, not in any file in /home/leo/src/reify. I grepped /home/leo/src/reify/scripts for `tail -N` used with extra arguments or multiple files and found nothing. No tracked file in this tree produces, teaches or fails to guard against it. The cause lies in agent-side command construction, which this tree does not contain.

The escalation MCP server belongs to dark-factory, so no file in this tree produces or fails to guard against the confusion.

The agent ran a `cat ... | tail -5` style command on the output of a background task, using the obsolete `-N` form with multiple file operands or after other options. GNU tail rejects this with 'option used in invalid context'. The command exited 1 even though every awaited step had reported rc=0, so the outcome looks like a failure and invites needless retries. Using `tail -n 5` would avoid it. Verifier: The cluster describes an ad-hoc agent-issued shell command (`cat ... | tail -5` on background task output) that GNU tail rejected. That is agent tooling behaviour. No file in /home/leo/src/reify produces or teaches the failure. The only grep hits for `tail -N` in this tree are single-input pipelines in tests/infra scripts, where the legacy form is valid, plus codebook entries. I did not inspect those hits individually, and I did not find the original multi-file invocation, so I could not confirm the cluster against the current tree.
